title: Taming nonlinear energy diffusion: The case of time-crystal energy condensates
abstract: We study a bulk-driven nonlinear variant of the Kipnis-Marchioro-Presutti model of stochastic energy diffusion in which local collisions are biased to induce a net energy flow, resembling the effect of an external field. Starting from the microscopic master equation, we derive the hydrodynamic description of the driven system via a local equilibrium approximation, obtaining explicit expressions for the energy current and the associated diffusivity and mobility transport coefficients, which are nonlinear functions of the local energy density. We test our findings in kinetic Monte Carlo simulations of the model and, as a proof of concept, we demonstrate the versatility of this driving mechanism to control nonlinear energy transport by inducing time-crystalline phases. In particular, we show that appropriately designed packing fields induce the spontaneous formation of traveling energy condensates, exhibiting robust long-range temporal order reminiscent of continuous time crystals. Our results provide a simple yet powerful framework to study bulk-driven nonlinear energy diffusion in stochastic many-body systems, offering a bridge between microscopic dynamics, macroscopic transport, and controlled spatiotemporal order.
summary: This paper develops a theoretical framework to study nonlinear energy diffusion driven internally within a many-body system, using a modified KMP model. By applying an engineered bulk driving field, the authors show they can actively control energy transport and induce stable, time-crystalline condensates. This offers a powerful tool for understanding and engineering non-equilibrium dynamics in complex physical media.
main_problem: The study focuses on controlling nonlinear energy diffusion in stochastic many-body systems by implementing a bulk driving mechanism, moving beyond traditional boundary-driven approaches.
main_result: The work demonstrates that appropriately designed external fields can induce the spontaneous formation of traveling energy condensates exhibiting robust long-range temporal order, characteristic of continuous time crystals.
method: The analysis derives the hydrodynamic description from a microscopic master equation using a local equilibrium approximation and validates findings via kinetic Monte Carlo simulations.
model_or_system: The system is a bulk-driven nonlinear variant of the Kipnis-Marchioro-Presutti (KMP) model for stochastic energy diffusion on a 1D lattice, where collisions are biased to induce a net energy flow in the bulk.
key_observables: Energy current, diffusivity $D(ho)$, mobility $\sigma(ho)$, and the formation/evolution of traveling energy condensates.
important_parameters: The external driving field strength ($\chi$ or $E$), local energy density ($ho$), and parameters controlling the packing fields ($\lambda_m$).
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on the local equilibrium approximation, and the hydrodynamic limit ($L 	o \infty$) is taken for macroscopic descriptions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate condensate profile evolution under varying driving strengths ($ eta$), showing critical points signaling structure emergence, and spatiotemporal raster plots demonstrating steady-state trajectories with multiple packing fields applied.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the microscopic master equation for bulk-driven diffusion to deriving macroscopic transport coefficients via local equilibrium approximation. It then applies this framework to show how engineered driving fields can stabilize time-crystalline phases, culminating in a discussion of systematic control over energy dynamics.
why_interesting: The connection between controlled non-equilibrium driving (the 'packing field') and the emergence of long-range temporal order (time crystals) provides a powerful analogy for engineering coherent quantum states or controlling dissipation in open quantum systems.
